transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Did you use any black dyes?

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: Logwood. That was quite complicated. I had to prepare the fabric so the dye would take.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: I hope you were careful to wear gloves.

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: Yes. I know the danger with that dye.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. It can be extremely dangerous if it’s ingested.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Now, presumably you had a look at an insect-based dye? Like cochineal, for example?

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: Yes. I didn’t actually make that, I didn’t have time to start crushing up insects to get the red colour  and anyway they’re not available here, but I managed to get the dye quite easily from a website. But it cost a fortune. I can see why it’s generally just used in cooking, and in small quantities.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Yes, it’s very effective, but that’s precisely why it’s not used as a dye.

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: I also read about using metal oxide. Apparently you can allow iron to rust while it’s in contact with the fabric, and that colours it.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Yes, that works well for dyeing cotton. But you have to be careful as the metal can actually affect the fabric and so you can’t expect to get a lot of wear out of fabrics treated in this way. And the colours are quite subtle, not everyone likes them. Anyway, it looks as if you’ve done a lot of work …
